craft_claim: Indian literary traditions carry a distinctly licensed, register-directed irreverence — hasya energy aimed at clerical pretension and ritual display from within devotion — so the tone is neither Anglophone-specific nor secular-only.

supporting_evidence.location: Introduction p. xvi; Poem XXI pp. 28-29; Poems LXV-LXVII pp. 68-71; Poem LXIX pp. 72-73
supporting_evidence.note: The Tagore-Underhill introduction frames Kabir as denouncing the apparatus of piety surrounding his tradition; the poems mock priestly garb, rosary, ceremonial thread, idol-worship, and ritual bathing, and stage a wonder-working friar's piety turned ironic — anticlerical ridicule voiced by a devotee, not a skeptic.

supporting_evidence.location: Work record (analysis_status: complete; locators verified this session)
supporting_evidence.note: The verse collection demonstrates the register machinery end to end: fervor held steady while the targets are religious professionals and outward observance — irreverence coexisting with devotion.

supporting_evidence.location: Frame verified via Project Gutenberg ebook #2400 record; tales not inspected
supporting_evidence.note: The riddle-cycle frame (twenty-five attempts, sanctioned impertinence toward a king) corroborates a South Asian tradition of rule-governed licensed mockery — frame-level, partial support only.

counterevidence.note: All evidence is translation-mediated (1915 English verse; source language behind the mediation unverified); locators refer to that edition, and the reception of Kabir's register in Hindi/Bhakti performance was not examined.

The Natyashastra's hasya (comic sentiment) chapter locator — commonly cited as chapter 6 — was NOT verified in this research session, so no classical taxonomic claim about hasya is made here; the shared record clm-rasa-emotional-aesthetic / src-natyashastra-ghosh-1951 is cross-linked read-only instead. Recorded as evidence-incomplete, alongside two further unfound anchors: a peer-reviewed source for Mulla-Nasruddin-in-India, and any scholarly source for the Birbal anecdote tradition.

scope: Indian/regional traditions speaking from inside a devotional or traditional frame while ridiculing religious professionals and outward piety; the license derives from the tradition's own prophetic or comic idiom.
exceptions: The claim is about tradition-level practice, not a universal Indian sensibility — it is grounded in the Kabir evidence specifically, not in a civilizational generalization.
Where the satire turns from clerical pretension to a program of reform against named institutions, it crosses into satirical-literature.
